newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, Taiwan, HK stocks rise despite Deng news.
newsitem.headline: China, Taiwan, HK stocks rise despite Deng news.

text.p: Stock markets in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan moved higher on Thursday after gyrating wildly at the opening following overnight news of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Hong Kong stocks had jumped 1.96 percent by midday, or 256.96 points, after an initial loss of 92 points.
"Investors feel that the last detectable uncertainty in China has been removed with the death of Deng Xiaoping," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities.

Reaction in U.S. markets had been muted, with the Dow Jones Industrials shedding 47.33 points to 7,020.13. Many other Asian markets also showed little response to the news, focusing instead on domestic considerations.
Tokyo shares soared nearly 500 points on investor enthusiasm over a Japanese newspaper report that the government may use public funds to help clear problem loans at the country's banks.
B share indices in both Shanghai and Shenzhen were slightly up after dropping by nearly the 10 percent limit in the first few minutes after the markets opened.
The Shanghai foreign-currency B index was up 0.29 percent or 0.188 points at 65.318 while Shenzhen was up 0.63 percent or 0.89 points at 142.64.

Alex Conroy, stock analyst with ING Barings in Shanghai, said the initial fall and subsequent rebound in the aftermath of Deng's death had long been expected, but the speed of the reaction was surprising.
"It's happening a bit faster than I expected," she said.
In Taiwan, the government moved swiftly to foster stability in its market following Deng's death.
The central bank said it will inject funds into the banking system to ensure sufficient liquidity and a government spokesman said it was prepared to support financial markets.
The weighted index rebounded from an earlier fall to close 21.19 points, or 0.28 percent higher at 7,678.04.

Thai stocks powered ahead as bargain hunters went after inexpensive blue-chip stocks. Traders said they had already discounted the news of Deng's death because there had been so many recent rumours concerning his health.
The SET index rose 27.77 points, or 3.80 percent, to 759.51.
Traders said Malaysian stocks were unfazed by Deng's death and moved higher as a result of a consolidation in small-capitalization stocks.
The Composite Index ended the morning 7.46 points higher, or 0.59 percent, at 1,269.91.
Singapore stocks rebounded from morning lows and were higher at midday, with the Straits Times index up 9.67 points, or 0.43 percent, at 2,256.66.
Australian shares followed Wall Street, ending lower on profit-taking. Traders said Deng's death was not a market factor.
The All Ordinaries share index was off 14.7 points, or 0.59 percent at 2,476.30.
Similarly, in New Zealand, stocks ended off their lows, with Deng's death having no impact. The market finished down 3.50 points, or 0.15 percent, at 2,325.85.

Deng's death had little impact on the foreign exchange market, although the U.S. dollar did weaken against the yen on speculative selling. The dollar was quoted at 123.72 after tounching a high of 124.62 in Tokyo.
"As far as the foreign exchange market is concerned, Deng's been dead for two or three years anyway," one trader said.
Gold markets in Asia also shrugged off the news of Deng's death, and focused on robust demand and tight supplies.
The key gold price in Hong Kong opened at US$344.60/345.10 an ounce, slightly below New York's close of $345.00/50 on Wednesday.
